think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 67-year-old Sri Lankan man with a 5-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine presented with a 2-month history of a painless, lobulated wrist and volar forearm mass causing carpal tunnel syndrome, in the complete absence of fever, weight loss, or pulmonary symptoms. The diagnostic tension lies in distinguishing an opportunistic tuberculous tenosynovitis (unmasked by immunosuppressive DMARD therapy) from a typical rheumatoid flexor tenosynovial flare or a benign soft-tissue neoplasm such as tenosynovial giant cell tumor.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Outpatient evaluation, neurophysiologic testing, wrist radiography, ultrasound, and contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrating multilobulated flexor tenosynovitis with median nerve compression, strictly prior to surgical tenosynovectomy, histopathologic evaluation, and Lowenstein-Jensen mycobacterial culture.
3. Differential Distinctions: Rheumatoid tenosynovitis commonly causes florid synovial proliferation in the carpal canal in patients with RA, but typically shows sterile lymphocytic pannus with non-caseating fibrinoid changes rather than necrotizing caseous granulomas with positive cultures. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor exhibits diffuse nodular synovial thickening without bony destruction, but histology demonstrates mononuclear cells, hemosiderin-laden histiocytes, and osteoclast-type giant cells without caseating necrosis.
case_prompt:
A 67-year-old Sri Lankan male with a 5-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis well-controlled on methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine presented with a 2-month history of a progressively enlarging, painless swelling of the left wrist accompanied by paresthesias and numbness involving the radial aspect of the left hand. He denied cough, dyspnea, fever, night sweats, anorexia, or unintentional weight loss. He was a lifetime non-smoker with an unremarkable personal and family medical history.

On physical examination, a lobulated, non-tender subcutaneous mass was palpated along the volar aspect of the distal forearm extending distally into the palmar region. There was no demonstrable thenar muscle atrophy, though mild reduction in active finger flexion was observed. Tinel's sign and Phalen's maneuver were positive over the left median nerve at the wrist. The remainder of the musculoskeletal and upper limb examination was unremarkable.

Basic hematologic and biochemical laboratory parameters were within reference limits, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 30 mm/hr. Nerve conduction studies demonstrated delayed sensory and motor latencies of the median nerve across the carpal tunnel, confirming moderately severe carpal tunnel syndrome. Plain radiographs of the left wrist showed no erosive or lytic bone lesions. Wrist ultrasound revealed marked lobulated synovial thickening enveloping the flexor tendons. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the hand and distal forearm demonstrated prominent enhancing synovial thickening with internal cystic foci tracking along the flexor tendons from the distal forearm through the carpal canal into the deep palm, without associated bony destruction. A high-resolution CT of the chest showed basilar interstitial fibrosis and pleural thickening consistent with rheumatoid-associated lung disease, without apical fibrosis, cavitary lesions, or consolidation.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered the most probable initial diagnosis given the patient's longstanding history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis presenting with florid flexor synovial hypertrophy causing secondary carpal tunnel syndrome; ruled out when surgical excision revealed caseating granulomas and mycobacterial growth rather than sterile inflammatory pannus.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Synovial thickening due to rheumatoid arthritis was considered the probable diagnosis, and surgical exploration for the decompression of carpal tunnel was planned.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor / Pigmented villonodular synovitis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the indolent, slowly progressive, mass-like lobulated synovial expansion tracking along the tendon sheaths through the carpal canal without bony erosion on plain radiographs; ruled out by histopathology demonstrating necrotizing caseous granulomas and positive microbial cultures.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Ultrasound scan of the wrist and distal forearm showed lobulated synovial thickening in relation to flexor tendons. His x-ray of the wrist did not show any features to suggest bony lesions.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Histopathological examination of the excised synovial mass revealed caseating granulomatous necrosis with Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells, and synovial tissue culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium with immunochromatographic MPT64 assay definitively confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The histology revealed a gelatinous mass with septated myxoid material, and surrounding wall contained granulomas with caseating type necrosis and Langhan-type giant cells suggestive of TB (Figure 4). The culture of the sample in Lowenstein Jensen culture medium with colony morphology and immunochromatographic identification test (MPT 64) was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

editor_comments: Clean admission presentation stopping prior to surgical tenosynovectomy and microbiological culture. All pathogen mentions purged from case prompt.
